pr.title: Finish a release that stopped halfway when the workflow runs again
pr.head: b14107d0948a89f8a4288c4eda08d92eb7f3dd41

summary: Projector ships each release through its Release workflow. When a pull request that raises the version merges to main, the workflow's publish job runs .github/scripts/release.py. That script pushes the version tag, such as v0.7.18, and force-moves the major tag v0 to the same commit. The installer, project upgrade, and every repository's site action follow v0. The script then creates the GitHub release, and the job asks the site workflow to rebuild.

Before this change, a release that failed partway could not be finished. The script's released command asked only whether the version tag existed, and tag refused once it did. So when GitHub accepted the version tag but rejected the v0 push, v0 stayed on the previous release, no GitHub release existed, and a re-run of the job called the version released and did nothing.
This change defines a version as released only when three things hold, and lets tag do whichever of them is missing:

1. The version tag exists on the remote.
  2. v0 names the same commit as the version tag, comparing the commit each annotated tag points to.
  3. The GitHub release exists.

Once the version tag exists, its commit is the release commit, so a resumed release finishes there even after main has moved on. A version tag that cannot belong to the version main names makes both commands exit 1 without moving anything.

cards.title: Terms on this page
cards.html:
• Version tag: the immutable vX.Y.Z tag a release pushes once.
  • Major tag: v0, force-moved to each new release; consumers follow it.
  • Peeled commit: the commit an annotated tag object points to. git ls-remote lists it as refs/tags/NAME^{}.
  • Release commit: the commit the release tags, which is main's head until the version tag exists and the tagged commit after.
  • Publish job: the Release workflow job that runs on a pyproject.toml push to main.

cards.title: What released answers
cards.html:
Remote stateExitPublish job does
All three parts in place0Stops on the first attempt; on a re-run, asks the site to rebuild
Any part missing3Runs tag, then asks the site to rebuild
Version tag cannot belong to this version, or git or gh failed1Fails the step

cards.title: Review so far
cards.html: The Projector review of b14107d found the head clean, with no finding threads. It left two documentation suggestions, noted on docs/plugins.md below.

groups.title: The release script reads the remote's state and finishes what is missing
intro: release.py holds both commands the publish job runs. merged fetches main and its tags, reads the version main names, and asks the remote with git ls-remote which commit the version tag and v0 each point to. It returns that state as Merged.

released turns that state, plus a gh release view lookup, into a list of missing parts; an empty list means exit 0. tag walks the same three parts in order and does only the missing ones. On failure, its error lists what it already did and says to run it again.

check_tagged guards the resume. Once a version tag exists, the script trusts it only when main contains the tagged commit and every commit from there to the head that touched a version file still names the same version. That stops v0 from moving back to an old commit after a release is reverted, or reverted and bumped again.

files.note: Defines the released state and makes tag idempotent: each step runs only when the remote lacks it.

checks.text: published treats only gh's release not found message as absent. Any other failure, such as missing auth, raises, so released exits 1 instead of reporting a release as missing.

The refs/tags/NAME^{} patterns return peeled commits from GitHub over HTTPS. Running git ls-remote --tags origin with them on this repository showed v0 and v0.7.18 both peeling to 704e570, so today's release reads as complete under the new rule.
This walk reads git log TAG..HEAD limited to the version files. A merge commit could bring side-branch commits naming an older version into that range, but this repository allows only squash merges.
--force matters for a local re-run: the failed run left a local v0 that the remote refused, and a plain tag fetch refuses to overwrite it.
The local tag is forced, but the push on the next line is not, so a version tag already on the remote is never replaced. Only v0's push uses --force.

groups.title: The publish job re-requests the site rebuild on a re-run
intro: The publish job runs released and branches on its exit code. Exit 3 now runs tag inside the case; the step then falls through to the repository_dispatch that rebuilds the site. Exit 0 still stops on the first attempt. On a re-run, where GITHUB_RUN_ATTEMPT is above 1, it falls through to the rebuild request too, because the attempt it repeats may have failed after tag and before that request.

files.note: Moves tag into the exit-3 branch and sends the rebuild request on a re-run whose release is already complete.

checks.text: Ran this case in bash under set -euo pipefail with stand-ins: exit 0 stops on attempt 1 and dispatches on attempt 2, exit 3 runs tag then dispatches, a failing tag stops the step, and exit 1 fails it.

groups.title: Tests run each release state against a local remote
groups.kicker: A bare Git remote and a fake gh stand in for GitHub
intro: TagTests builds a temporary repository with a local bare remote and puts a fake gh on PATH that keeps its releases in a file. A pre-receive hook on the remote that rejects v0 reproduces the failure this change fixes.

files.note: Covers a fresh release, the resume after a failed v0 push or a failed GitHub release, the complete state, and the three refusals.

checks.text: All 18 tests pass at this head with Python 3.12, and the full suite of 926 tests passes with 1 skipped.
This is the scenario the pull request exists for: the version tag lands, v0 is refused, main moves on, and the next tag moves v0 to the tagged commit rather than the newer head.

groups.title: Documentation says how to finish a stopped release
intro: Both documents now define a released version by its three parts and tell you to re-run the failed job, or run tag again, to finish one that stopped partway.

files.note: Rewrites the release section around the three-part definition, the resume, and the refusals.

checks.text: Review suggestion: tag --no-release never calls gh, so "both commands need an authenticated gh" holds only for released and a tag that creates the release.

Review suggestion: running tag by hand does not ask the site workflow to rebuild. Only the publish job sends that request, so after a hand-run tag the site keeps the old action until the job is re-run.

files.note: Adds one sentence: re-run the publish job when it fails partway.
